class.name: NetwQuantizeScalar
class.brief_description: [NetwQuantize] that snaps a number, or each axis of a [Vector2] or [Vector3], onto a uniform grid across a bounded range.
class.description:
The grid is one number said two ways, and the class publishes both: [member bit_count] is the wire budget and [member resolution_step] is the precision it buys. Writing either derives the other from [member min_limit] and [member max_limit], so tuning a property by asking for 19 bits and tuning it by asking for 3cm of precision are the same act on the same object rather than two classes to choose between. [codeblock] var q := NetwQuantizeScalar.new().limits(-2048.0, 2048.0).bits(19)
# the same grid, said the other way, and the swap is one word: var q := NetwQuantizeScalar.new().limits(-2048.0, 2048.0).step(0.0078) [/codeblock] [b]Declare the limits before the step.[/b] [member resolution_step] is a request rather than a stored field: setting it picks the smallest [member bit_count] whose grid is at least that fine over the range currently declared, so a step written before its limits is derived against the wrong range. [method bits] is exact at any point in a chain. A [Vector3] or [Vector2] quantizes each axis the same way and costs [member bit_count] bits per axis. The per-axis error is at most half [member resolution_step]. Only the three stored fields decide the layout, so two of these that address the same grid return [code]true[/code] to [method NetwQuantize.is_same_layout] however each was authored.

method.name: bits
method.description: Builder that sets [member bit_count] and returns this quantizer.

method.name: limits
method.description: Builder that sets [member min_limit] and [member max_limit] and returns this quantizer. It leaves [member bit_count] alone, so widening the range on a fixed budget coarsens [member resolution_step] rather than spending more bits.

method.name: step
method.description: Builder that asks for a grid at least as fine as [param step] over the current range, by raising [member bit_count] to suit, and returns this quantizer. Declare [method limits] first.

members.member: Bits spent per axis, clamped to 1..32. This is the stored knob and the wire budget: the range is divided into [code]2 ** bit_count - 1[/code] equal steps, so a value at either limit round-trips exactly.
Inclusive upper bound of the encoded range. A value above it is clamped rather than wrapped, which is why an angle takes [NetwQuantizeAngle] instead.
Inclusive lower bound of the encoded range. A value below it is clamped.

Distance between two adjacent grid points, DERIVED from the other three rather than stored: reading it returns [code](max_limit - min_limit) / (2 ** bit_count - 1)[/code], and writing it moves [member bit_count] to the smallest budget that is at least that fine. A step of zero or less is rejected, because no bit count satisfies it.
